data.full_text:
Top Cloud-Based Practice Management Software for Dental Practices

So, you’re considering making the switch to a cloud-based practice management software for your dental practice. That’s great and we clearly understand the intrigue... especially because cloud is all the rage these days. But with a crowded market — and every vendor website saying the same things: all-in-one, intuitive, cloud-native, scalable. It can get a little overwhelming. So we did the digging for you. We looked at four of the most talked-about cloud-based practice management systems right now — CareStack, Curve Dental, Denticon, and Dentrix Ascend — and put together an honest, non-biased breakdown: what each system does, what real users are saying in verified reviews, and who each one is genuinely the best fit for. And, as a dental IT provider who has experience troubleshooting and working with cloud PMS... we’ve included some critical considerations as you explore moving your dental practice to a cloud practice management system. There's no ranked list (their in alphabetical order) or winner here. The right PMS for a private general dental practice in Phoenix looks very different from the right solution for a 10-location dental organization on the East Coast.

Looking for a broader dental practice management software comparison that includes server-based or hybrid systems like Dentrix, Eaglesoft, and Open Dental? We covered those - including a full list of dental software programs across deployment types - in our previous article: Top Practice Management Software for Dental Practices. This article focuses specifically on cloud-first solutions for practices ready to leave the server behind. What to Look for in a Cloud-Based Dental PMS Before we get into the individual systems, here are the factors worth weighing as you compare: True cloud vs. cloud-hosted: Is it built for the cloud from the ground up, or is it a legacy system running through a remote desktop?

Ease of use and training time: A powerful system no one knows how to use is a liability, not an asset.

Integrations: Does it work with your imaging software, payment processor, and patient communication tools... or will you be managing a patchwork of add-ons?

Reporting and analytics: Can you get the numbers you need without needing a degree in data science to run a report?

Support quality: What does onboarding look like? What happens when something goes wrong at 3PM on a Wednesday?

Scalability: Will this system grow with you, or will you outgrow it in two years?

Total cost of ownership: Monthly fees are just the beginning. Factor in onboarding, training, add-ons, and data export.

Data portability: If you ever need to switch, can you get your patient records out without a fight? Whether you're new to evaluating dental software programs or you're coming off a legacy system and ready to modernize, these criteria apply regardless of which platform you're considering. CareStack Website: carestack.com

G2 Rating: 4.7/5 (176 reviews)

Software Advice Rating: 4.8/5 (189 reviews) Overview CareStack is an all-in-one, cloud-based dental practice management platform built to serve everything from single-office practices to large, enterprise-level DSOs. The software covers scheduling, clinical charting, treatment planning, billing, revenue cycle management (RCM), patient communications, and analytics — all without the need for third-party add-ons. More than 2,500 dental practices across the U.S. use CareStack. It holds the #1 ranking on G2 for dental practice management software, is certified in HIPAA, SOC 2 Type 2, and ISO 27001:2022, and has been the subject of a Forrester Total Economic Impact™ study that suggests the platform can pay for itself within six months for multi-location practices. CareStack has also been actively expanding its AI capabilities — including AI-driven telephony (VoiceStack™) and AI-powered imaging analysis (Aeka™). What CareStack Users Say "I have been working with CareStack for over 4 years, and the team is amazing — very professional and knowledgeable. The PMS offers comprehensive systems that enable practices to grow both internally and externally, making it an excellent solution for DSOs." — G2 Verified Review "There is a bit of a learning curve at first because the system has so many features. Once you get used to it, though, it becomes much easier to navigate." — G2 Verified Review Pros Truly all-in-one: scheduling, charting, billing, patient communications, RCM, and analytics in a single platform with no required add-ons

Strong multi-location capabilities: centralized reporting and cross-practice operations from one dashboard

Excellent customer support and onboarding: consistently cited as a differentiator in user reviews

Active product development: users report seeing their feature requests implemented

AI-powered growth tools available as part of the ecosystem (VoiceStack™, Aeka™) Cons Steeper learning curve: the depth of features requires meaningful investment in training, especially for teams new to cloud software

Implementation timeline: onboarding can take approximately two months, and some features have been flagged as still "in development" at go-live

Billing workflows can feel multi-step: some users note that billing processes require more clicks than comparable systems

Pricing requires a custom quote: not publicly listed, which makes early budgeting harder

Dependent on internet connectivity: like all cloud systems, a downed connection means disrupted workflow until it's restored Best Suited For CareStack is an excellent fit for growth-oriented practices — whether that's a single office planning to expand, a multi-location group looking to standardize operations, or a DSO that needs enterprise-level visibility and scalability. If your goal is to reduce your vendor count and gain real-time cross-location reporting, CareStack deserves a close look. That said, if your team is small and you need to be up and running quickly without a significant learning curve, the feature depth may feel like more than you need right now. Curve Dental Website: curvedental.com

G2 Rating: 4.6/5 (165 reviews)

Software Advice Rating: 4.4/5 (285 reviews) Overview Curve Dental is one of the original cloud-native dental practice management platforms — built for the cloud from day one, not adapted to it after the fact. This means the system was designed around the realities of browser-based access, mobile flexibility, and continuous delivery of updates — not retrofitted from a legacy product. Trusted by over 80,000 dental professionals across practices of all sizes, Curve offers a comprehensive suite: scheduling, charting, billing, patient intake, treatment planning, automated insurance verification, membership plans, and dashboard reporting — all in one platform. The company also claims customers report up to 20% higher collections, 25% more new patients, and 30% better case acceptance after adopting the system. Curve has also introduced a Curve Mobile experience and continues to integrate AI partners like Pearl and Bola AI for imaging and treatment acceptance improvements. Cloud-only which means full internet dependency

Unlike platforms that started as single-practice solutions and scaled up, Denticon was designed from the beginning to handle the operational complexity of enterprise dental organizations — centralized scheduling, cross-location reporting, multi-specialty workflows, and consolidated RCM at scale. Used by more than 13,000 dental practices, including notable DSO brands like Park Dental, Smile Brands, D4C, and Dental Care Alliance, Denticon positions itself as the operational backbone for high-growth dental businesses. The platform includes a full suite of clinical, front office, and reporting tools, as well as newer additions like AI Voice Perio charting, AI Voice Restorative charting, and AI Assist for proactive patient treatment insights. Planet DDS also offers Apteryx XVWeb — a cloud-based dental imaging solution that integrates directly with Denticon, providing a companion to the practice management platform. What Denticon Users Say "In the last 10 years of using Planet DDS, we have grown from 2 to 11 locations. The ease of use of the product is unmatched. The conversion process is seamless, and the support team is phenomenal." — G2 Verified Review Pros Purpose-built for multi-location and DSO operations: centralized visibility, reporting, and management across all locations from a single platform

Comprehensive RCM tools: batch claims, automated eligibility verification (AutoEligibility), 835 auto-posting, and revenue dashboards

Strong implementation and data conversion support: Planet DDS has experience converting data from nearly every PMS

Morning Huddle dashboard: a standout feature that helps teams start the day aligned on production goals and schedule priorities

Proven track record with enterprise clients: 20+ years in market, with large DSO references Cons Interface can feel dated: multiple users note the UI could benefit from a visual refresh, though Planet DDS acknowledges ongoing work here

Analytics learning curve: while reporting is powerful, some users find the analytics setup complex to configure correctly

Not ideal for solo or small single-location practices: the feature depth and complexity is calibrated for larger organizations Best Suited For Denticon is the right platform for multi-location dental groups, growing DSOs, and enterprise dental organizations that need a cloud-based system capable of handling real operational scale. If you're managing multiple providers and locations, need centralized RCM, and are evaluating against other DSO-grade platforms, Denticon belongs on your shortlist. For smaller, independent single-location practices, the complexity and pricing model may be more than what you need. Lighter, more accessible platforms like Curve Dental or CareStack may serve you better. Dentrix Ascend Website: dentrixascend.com

G2 Rating: 4.3/5 (18 reviews)

Software Advice Rating: 4.1/5 (234 reviews) Overview Dentrix Ascend is the cloud-based evolution of Dentrix — one of the most established names in dental practice management software. Built by Henry Schein One, Ascend takes the brand recognition and deep dental industry roots of legacy Dentrix and moves them into a fully cloud-native environment. The platform covers scheduling, billing, clinical charting, imaging, AI-powered diagnostics, patient communications, and real-time analytics. Dental Practice Management Tools Market Summary



Dental practice management tools are specialized software solutions designed for dental clinics, hospital dentistry departments, and multi-location dental groups. These platforms serve as the operational backbone of modern dental practices, integrating appointment scheduling, electronic health records, billing, treatment planning, imaging management, and patient communications into a unified digital ecosystem. Their core purpose is to enhance clinical efficiency, elevate patient experience, standardize workflows, and provide actionable business intelligence for informed decision-making.



Market Outlook



The global dental practice management tools market is projected to reach USD 3.51 billion by 2032, growing at a compound annual growth rate (CAGR) of 9.5%. This robust growth reflects the accelerating digital transformation across dental care delivery, driven by rising patient expectations, operational complexity, and the imperative for data-driven practice management.



Competitive Landscape



The market is moderately concentrated, with the top ten global players accounting for approximately 50.0% of total revenue. Key solution providers include Dentrix, Planet DDS, CareStack, Eaglesoft, and Open Dental-each offering differentiated capabilities spanning on-premise deployments, cloud-native architectures, and specialty-specific functionality.



Key Market Drivers



1. Rising Complexity of Dental Practice Operations

Growing consumer awareness of oral health, increasing disposable incomes, and expanded insurance coverage have fueled demand for higher-value dental services-including orthodontics, implants, and aesthetic restorations. Practices have evolved from single-provider, basic-treatment models to multi-provider, multi-service operations. Patient scheduling, clinical documentation, imaging integration, inventory tracking, and insurance billing have become increasingly complex. Traditional manual methods or basic spreadsheet tools can no longer support the accuracy, efficiency, and compliance required, compelling practices to adopt professional management platforms.



2. Patient Experience as a Competitive Differentiator

In the increasingly competitive private dental market, patients evaluate practices not only on clinical outcomes but also on convenience, transparency, and communication quality. Modern management tools enhance patient experience through automated appointment reminders, online booking and payment portals, visualized treatment plans, and structured follow-up protocols. Positive patient experiences drive higher retention rates, referrals, and lifetime value-prompting practice owners to view management software as essential infrastructure for customer relationship management rather than a discretionary expense.



3. Cloud Adoption and Multi-Site Scalability

The rapid expansion of dental group practices and franchised networks has created demand for centralized management capabilities. Headquarters require real-time visibility into patient volumes, provider productivity, inventory levels, and financial performance across multiple locations to optimize resource allocation, ensure brand consistency, and control costs. Legacy on-premise systems cannot deliver this cross-site intelligence. Cloud-based platforms, with their centralized databases, role-based access controls, and consolidated reporting, have become indispensable enablers of scalable growth-driving investment from mid-sized and large dental organizations.



Market Restraints



1. Cost Sensitivity Among Small Practices

A significant portion of dental practices remain independently owned with constrained operating budgets. While cloud-based subscription models reduce upfront capital expenditure, recurring monthly or annual fees are still perceived as a financial burden-particularly during periods of patient volume fluctuations or economic uncertainty. This price sensitivity can prolong sales cycles and limit penetration among smaller, single-location practices.



2. Clinician-Centric Decision-Making

In many dental practices, the primary decision-makers are practicing clinicians who prioritize clinical techniques and patient outcomes over administrative infrastructure. Operational management, workflow optimization, and back-office efficiency may not receive the same level of attention as investments in clinical equipment. This focus gap can delay adoption decisions and requires vendors to effectively communicate the clinical and operational value proposition to dentist-owners.



Strategic Outlook



The dental practice management tools market is positioned at the convergence of healthcare digitization, consumerization of dental services, and the consolidation of private practices. As patient expectations shift toward seamless, transparent, and connected care experiences, and as multi-location groups seek integrated operational control, the demand for cloud-native, AI-enhanced, and interoperable platforms will intensify. Vendors that combine intuitive user experience, robust analytics, and specialized dental workflows-while addressing the distinct needs of both solo practitioners and enterprise groups-will capture disproportionate share in this rapidly evolving market.

Weighing up the high cost of SMS reminders with lost practice time is a tricky balance – Adrian Dray at CareStack explores whether SMS messages can be used in a financially sustainable way and the potential alternatives.

Practice owners are absolutely right to be obsessed with reducing failed-to-attend (FTA) rates and white space in the diary. That is where profitability, stability, and patient continuity live.

So why are so many practices switching off one of their most effective tools? And what needs to change for UK dentistry?

As a patient, if you do not send me an SMS reminder, there is a strong chance I will miss my appointment. That is not a proud admission, it is reality. Life is noisy, work is busy, and most of us are conditioned to rely on short, clear prompts on our phones.

Think about how many organisations already do this well. Delivery services, subscription platforms, service providers, booking tools. they all lean on SMS to protect attendance, reduce friction, and keep revenue predictable. They understand that attention is fragmented, so reminders need to be direct and difficult to ignore.

Dental practices are no different.

What is the downside of SMS messaging?

The tension comes from SMS cost. If a practice is paying somewhere between 4p and 12p per SMS, the numbers add up quickly.

Take a typical example at 8p per message, sent through practice management software. A patient books an examination. They receive:

An SMS confirming the appointment

An SMS reminder one week before

An SMS with a link to complete medical history via the patient portal

An SMS one time password to access that portal

A final reminder the day before

A follow up SMS inviting them to leave a review.

By the time that journey is complete, the practice may have spent around 40p for one patient. On its own, that feels acceptable if it protects clinical time and generates a review. Translate that across hundreds or thousands of appointments each month, and it becomes a serious line on the profit and loss statement (P&L).

What are the alternatives to standard SMS reminders?

At this point, practices start searching for alternatives. Here is how the main strategies compare.

1. Switching to email reminders – rating: 3/5

Email is often ‘free’ at the point of use and feels like the obvious saving. The challenge is modern inbox filtering. Stronger spam controls, automatic categorisation, and cluttered inboxes mean reminder emails are easier to miss.

For practices with high FTA sensitivity, relying on email alone can be a calculated risk.

Tip: if you trial email only, ring fence a defined period, closely track FTA rates, rebooking behaviour, and short notice gaps, and be prepared to reverse the change quickly if performance drops.

2. Using third party messaging tools – rating: 3.5/5

Dedicated messaging platforms that connect with existing systems or use channels such as SMS and Whatsapp can improve flexibility or pricing.

Tip: check deliverability reports, confirm how patient data is processed, and review UK GDPR, data sharing, and retention responsibilities. A cheaper message that fails to arrive, or a tool that mishandles data, quickly erodes any perceived saving.

3. Choosing software with sustainable SMS pricing – rating: 4.5/5

For many organisations, the stronger long term move is to choose core software that bakes fair, transparent messaging into its model.

When a system includes a meaningful SMS allowance within the subscription, applies a low, predictable rate beyond that, and does not charge for essentials such as incoming replies or portal access codes, it becomes realistic to keep SMS switched on at scale. That means fewer empty chairs, stronger patient communication, and less anxiety about every reminder sent.

Where this is combined with integrated tools such as imaging, referrals, and reputation management, practices also reduce fragmentation and gain clearer visibility of both costs and outcomes. The higher rating reflects its balance of sustainability, control, and patient behaviour alignment.

The bigger point for UK dentistry is this. FTA reduction and diary optimisation depend on consistent, reliable communication. Turning off SMS purely because of opaque or inflated pricing puts practices at risk of empty chairs and lost trust. The smarter move is to interrogate your numbers, understand exactly how your current setup charges, and explore options that make it affordable to keep using the channels your patients actually respond to.

If SMS helps patients turn up, pay, and rebook, then pricing models should support it, not punish it.

6 Things to Consider When Choosing Orthodontic Software Choosing orthodontic software isn’t just about picking the most feature-packed option. It shouldn’t disrupt your existing workflow. It should integrate with your existing systems, and make things easier. Here’s what to keep in mind before committing to a solution: Ease of Use If a system slows you down, it’s not the right one. Some platforms boast impressive features. Their reps will sell you on the latest widgets and gizmos. But, they take weeks to figure out. The best software is intuitive, with clear workflows and a dashboard that makes sense from day one. It should feel familiar to you from day one. Integration with Existing Systems The last thing you need is software that requires you to buy more software. The best solutions integrate with what you already have. After all, manually transferring patient data between systems introduces an increased risk of errors. Look for a solution that integrates smoothly with your imaging software, practice management system, and billing tools. Cloud-Based vs. On-Premises Some clinicians want the flexibility of remote access. A cloud-based solution affords you that luxury. Plus, you won’t need to integrate bulky servers, (mind-numbingly slow) updates, and archaic technical support. However, if you prefer full control over data storage, an on-premises system might be a better fit. It comes down to what makes the most sense for how you run your practice. AI and Automation Capabilities The latest orthodontic software opens up a whole new world of automation. You can digitise treatment planning, optimize aligner staging, and even predict case progress. How much you wish to automate is a personal choice. But, it’s a worthwhile factor to consider if you hope to future-proof your practice in the coming decade. Security and Compliance Patient data security isn’t optional. Any software you choose should be HIPAA-compliant, offer encrypted storage, and give you control over who can access sensitive information. A data breach creates a serious liability, and causes you unnecessary headache as a clinic owner. Scalability and Support

Your software should grow with your practice. Whether you're expanding to multiple locations, adding more patients, or bringing on new staff, your system needs to keep up. And when you run into issues, you need responsive support that offers real solutions—not just a help center article or a list of FAQs. There’s a multitude of other factors that could be relevant to your practice. But, this is something you will need to consider over time.
